reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / WHO nutrition guidance
clinicalPearls: Wet beriberi presents with high-output cardiac failure, oedema, and warm extremities, whereas dry beriberi is a symmetrical peripheral polyneuropathy
Thiamine deficiency also causes Wernicke encephalopathy, with the triad of confusion, ophthalmoplegia, and ataxia, which can progress to irreversible Korsakoff amnesia
It is associated with diets based on polished (milled) white rice, chronic alcohol use, hyperemesis, bariatric surgery, and prolonged unsupplemented parenteral feeding
Infantile beriberi can occur in breastfed infants of thiamine-deficient mothers and may be acute and life-threatening
Thiamine should be given before or with any glucose load in at-risk patients, as glucose can precipitate acute Wernicke encephalopathy
A rapid improvement in cardiac output after thiamine strongly supports wet beriberi
Diagnosis is largely clinical, supported by the response to treatment, since laboratory confirmation may be slow
reference.pathophysiology: Thiamine, as thiamine pyrophosphate, is a cofactor for key enzymes of carbohydrate metabolism including pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and transketolase. Deficiency impairs oxidative energy production and causes accumulation of pyruvate and lactate, hitting tissues with high energy demand such as heart, peripheral nerves, and brain. Cardiovascular (wet) disease reflects impaired myocardial energetics and peripheral vasodilatation producing high-output failure, while neural (dry) disease and Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome reflect neuronal energy failure. Carbohydrate loading raises thiamine demand and can unmask or worsen deficiency.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of high-output or dilated cardiomyopathy
Other peripheral neuropathies such as diabetic or alcoholic neuropathy
Other causes of delirium and ataxia
Fluid overload from renal, hepatic, or cardiac disease
additionalInvestigations: Clinical assessment with dietary and alcohol history
Erythrocyte transketolase activity or blood thiamine level where available
Assessment of cardiac function in suspected wet beriberi
Neurological and cognitive assessment for Wernicke-Korsakoff features
Evaluation for coexisting deficiencies in the malnourished or alcohol-dependent
redFlags: Acute high-output cardiac failure or cardiovascular collapse (fulminant wet beriberi)
Wernicke encephalopathy, a medical emergency requiring immediate thiamine
Rapid deterioration in an infant with suspected infantile beriberi
Glucose administration in an at-risk patient without prior thiamine
reference.prognosis: Cardiac and early neurological features often improve rapidly with thiamine, but delayed treatment of Wernicke encephalopathy risks permanent Korsakoff amnesia, and severe peripheral neuropathy may recover only partially.
pitfalls: Giving intravenous glucose before thiamine in an at-risk patient and precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy
Failing to recognise high-output failure as a treatable nutritional cardiomyopathy
Waiting for laboratory confirmation before treating in suspected Wernicke encephalopathy
Overlooking deficiency after bariatric surgery, in hyperemesis, or on prolonged parenteral nutrition
management: Give parenteral thiamine replacement promptly as the definitive treatment for wet and dry beriberi and for Wernicke encephalopathy
Always administer thiamine before or with any glucose load in at-risk patients to avoid precipitating acute Wernicke encephalopathy
Support the failing circulation in wet beriberi while thiamine reverses the high-output state
Correct coexisting nutritional deficiencies and address the underlying cause such as alcohol dependence, hyperemesis or unsupplemented parenteral feeding
Provide dietary counselling and ongoing thiamine supplementation to prevent recurrence
Monitor cardiac and neurological recovery, recognising that delayed treatment risks irreversible Korsakoff amnesia and incomplete neuropathy recovery
Involve neurology, cardiology and dietetics and screen at-risk groups including breastfed infants of thiamine-deficient mothers
